units.title: Hello, OCaml!
units.summary: Write your first OCaml program and print text with print_endline, print_string and Printf.printf.

lesson.md: A program is a list of instructions for the computer. Your first instruction is `print_endline`: it prints a piece of text and then starts a new line. Text in OCaml is called a **string**, and you write it between double quotes, like `"Hello"`.

lesson.code: let () = print_endline "Hello, OCaml!"

lesson.md: The line starts with `let () =`. This means: run the code on the right side when the program starts. The `()` is a special value called **unit**. It means "nothing": `print_endline` prints something, but it gives back no useful value, only `()`.

To run several instructions one after the other, put a semicolon `;` between them. You put the semicolon between two instructions, not after the last one. OCaml does not care about line breaks or indentation, but the indentation of two spaces makes the code easy to read.

`print_string` prints text, but it does not start a new line. The next text continues on the same line. Inside a string, `\n` is a new line character, so `print_string "Hi\n"` prints `Hi` and then starts a new line.

`Printf.printf` prints text with placeholders. `%s` is a placeholder for a string and `%d` for a whole number. After the text you write the values for the placeholders, in the same order, separated by spaces. There are no commas and no parentheses around them.

lesson.code:
let () =
  Printf.printf "%s is %d years old\n" "Ada" 36

lesson.md: Like `print_string`, `Printf.printf` does not add a new line by itself. End the text with `\n` when you want the next output to start on a new line.

card: `\n` inside a string starts a new line

exercises.explain: The three `%d` placeholders get the values `2`, `3` and `5` in this order.

exercises.statement: `print_string` starts a new line after the text.
exercises.explain: Only `print_endline` adds a new line. With `print_string` you write `\n` yourself.

exercises.explain: `print_endline` ends the line after `Hello`. With `print_string` or `Printf.printf` you get `HelloWorld` on one line.

units.title: Values and types
units.summary: Give names to values with let and get to know int, float, string and bool.

lesson.md: `let` gives a name to a value. Here `age` is the name and `36` is the value. A name starts with a lowercase letter. After this line, you can use `age` everywhere below it in the program.

Inside a block of code, you write `let name = value in`. The word `in` means: the name exists in the code that follows. The parentheses in `(price * count)` turn the calculation into one value for the placeholder.

lesson.code:
let () =
  let price = 4 in
  let count = 3 in
  Printf.printf "%d\n" (price * count)

lesson.md: Every value has a **type**. Whole numbers like `3` have the type `int`, and numbers with a dot like `2.5` have the type `float`. For `int` you use `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. For `float` the operators have a dot: `+.`, `-.`, `*.` and `/.`. You print a `float` with `%f`, and `%.1f` prints it with one digit after the dot. Division of two `int` values gives a whole number: `7 / 2` is `3`. The operator `mod` gives the rest of the division: `7 mod 2` is `1`.
OCaml never mixes `int` and `float` by itself. `3 + 1.5` is an error, and so is `2.0 +. 1`. Convert first: `float_of_int 3` gives `3.`, the `float` version of `3`, and `int_of_float 2.9` gives `2`.
The operator `^` joins two strings into one. To put a number into a string, convert it with `string_of_int`. `String.length` gives the number of characters in a string.
A `bool` value is either `true` or `false`. You print it with the placeholder `%b`. In the next unit you use booleans to make decisions.
A value never changes. `let x = x + 1 in` does not change `x`: it creates a new `x` that hides the old one in the code that follows.

card: `let x = 5 in ...` gives a name to a value

exercises.explain: The second `let` creates a new `x` with the value `4 * 3`, which is `12`. Then `12 - 2` is `10`.

exercises.explain: 5 fits 3 times into 17, so `17 / 5` is `3`. The rest is `17 - 15`, so `17 mod 5` is `2`.

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions, call them with arguments, and use functions without a name.

lesson.md: A **function** turns input values into a result. `let square x = x * x` defines a function with the name `square` and one **parameter**, `x`. The code after `=` is the body. Its value is the result, so OCaml needs no `return`.

To call a function, write its name and then the argument, separated by a space: `square 5`. You need parentheses only to group things. A call comes before the other operators, so `square 2 + 3` means `(square 2) + 3`.
A function can have several parameters, separated by spaces. When you call it, you also separate the arguments with spaces, without commas.

OCaml finds the types of a function by itself. The type of `area` is `int -> int -> int`: it takes two `int` values and gives an `int`. The arrow `->` separates the inputs from the result. The type of `greet` is `string -> string`.
`fun x -> x * 2` is a function without a name. It takes `x` and gives `x * 2`. You can give it a name with `let`. `let double = fun x -> x * 2` is the same as `let double x = x * 2`.
When you give a function only its first argument, you get a new function that waits for the rest. This is called **partial application**. Here `add 10` is a function that adds `10` to its argument.

lesson.code:
let add a b = a + b

let () =
  let add_ten = add 10 in
  Printf.printf "%d %d\n" (add_ten 5) (add_ten 32)

lesson.md: A function that needs no input takes `()` as its parameter: `let say_hi () = print_endline "Hi"`. You call it with `say_hi ()`.

card: `let square x = x * x` defines a function
`let area w h = w * h` has the type `int -> int -> int`
`fun x -> x + 1` is a function without a name
`let add_ten = add 10` gives only the first argument

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Choose between values with if, then and else, compare values, and match a value against patterns.

lesson.md: `if condition then a else b` gives `a` when the condition is `true` and `b` when it is `false`. In OCaml, `if` is an **expression**: it has a value, like `2 + 3` has a value. Both branches must have the same type.

lesson.code:
let () =
  let temp = 25 in
  let text = if temp > 20 then "warm" else "cold" in
  print_endline text

lesson.md: You compare values with `=` (equal), `<>` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. The result is a `bool`. You combine conditions with `&&` (and) and `||` (or), and `not` turns `true` into `false` and back.
For more than two choices, put another `if` after `else`. OCaml checks the conditions from top to bottom and uses the first one that is `true`.
You can leave out `else` only when the `then` branch gives `()`, for example when it prints: `if n > 0 then print_endline "positive"`. In all other cases, `else` is required.

`match x with` compares a value with **patterns**, one after the other. Each case starts with `|`, then the pattern, `->` and the result. The first pattern that fits wins. The pattern `_` fits every value, so it usually comes last.
One case can have several patterns, separated by `|`. You can match strings, numbers, booleans and more.
OCaml also has `==` and `!=`, but they check something else. To compare two values, always use `=` and `<>`.

card: `if x > 0 then "pos" else "neg"` has a value

exercises.explain: 8 is not greater than 10, but it is greater than 5, so the second branch gives `medium`.

exercises.explain: `2` does not fit `0`, but it fits one of the patterns `1 | 2 | 3`.

units.title: Lists
units.summary: Store many values in a list, add and join lists, and work with every element using List functions.

lesson.md: A **list** holds several values of the same type, in order. You write it in square brackets and separate the elements with semicolons: `[1; 2; 3]`. `[]` is the empty list. A list of `int` values has the type `int list`.

The operator `::` puts one element in front of a list: `0 :: [1; 2]` is `[0; 1; 2]`. The operator `@` joins two lists. `List.length` gives the number of elements. Like all values, a list never changes: `::` and `@` create new lists.

lesson.code:
let () =
  let nums = [1; 2; 3] in
  let more = 0 :: nums in
  let all = more @ [4; 5] in
  Printf.printf "%d %d %d\n" (List.length nums) (List.length more) (List.length all)

lesson.md: `List.iter f list` calls the function `f` with every element, from first to last. It is useful for printing.
`List.map f list` calls `f` with every element and collects the results in a new list. A function without a name is handy here.

lesson.code:
let () =
  let nums = [1; 2; 3] in
  let doubled = List.map (fun x -> x * 2) nums in
  List.iter (fun x -> Printf.printf "%d\n" x) doubled

lesson.md: `List.filter f list` keeps only the elements for which `f` gives `true`. The order of the elements stays the same.

lesson.code:
let () =
  let nums = [5; 12; 8; 3; 20] in
  let big = List.filter (fun x -> x > 7) nums in
  List.iter (fun x -> Printf.printf "%d\n" x) big

lesson.md: `String.concat sep list` joins a list of strings into one string, with `sep` between the elements. Together with `List.map` and `string_of_int`, it prints a list of numbers on one line.
Use semicolons in lists, not commas. `[1, 2, 3]` is not a list of three numbers: it is a list with only one element, the group `1, 2, 3`.

card: `[1; 2; 3]` is a list, `[]` the empty list
`0 :: nums` adds in front, `a @ b` joins

units.title: Recursion
units.summary: Write functions that call themselves with let rec, take lists apart with patterns, and use accumulators.

lesson.md: A **recursive** function calls itself. In OCaml you define it with `let rec` instead of `let`. Without `rec`, the function cannot see its own name, and you get an error.

`factorial 5` is `5 * factorial 4`, and `factorial 4` is `4 * factorial 3`, and so on. When `n` reaches `1`, the function stops calling itself and gives `1`. This stopping point is the **base case**. The result is `5 * 4 * 3 * 2 * 1`, which is `120`.

Every list is either empty, `[]`, or a first element followed by the rest of the list, `head :: tail`. With `match` you handle both patterns. In the second case, the names `head` and `tail` get the first element and the rest.

`sum [3; 5; 7]` is `3 + sum [5; 7]`, then `3 + 5 + sum [7]`, then `3 + 5 + 7 + sum []`. The empty list is the base case and gives `0`. In the same way, a recursive function can build a new list with `::`.

An **accumulator** is an extra parameter that carries the result so far. Here the helper function `go` is defined inside `sum`. It adds each element to `acc`, and at the end of the list it gives `acc`. The call `go 0 list` starts with `0`. Because the recursive call is the last step, this version also works with very long lists.
When you do not need a value from a pattern, write `_` instead of a name: `| _ :: rest -> 1 + count rest` counts the elements without looking at them.
Every recursive function needs a base case, and each call must come closer to it. Otherwise the function calls itself again and again until the program crashes.

card: `let rec f n = ... f (n - 1) ...` calls itself
a base case stops the recursion
`let rec go acc xs = ...` carries the result in `acc`

units.title: Variants and records
units.summary: Define your own types: variants for values with several cases, and records for values with named fields.

lesson.md: With `type` you define your own type. A **variant** type lists all possible cases. Each case is a **constructor** and starts with an uppercase letter. A value of type `color` is always `Red`, `Green` or `Blue`, nothing else.

lesson.code:
type color = Red | Green | Blue

let name c =
  match c with
  | Red -> "red"
  | Green -> "green"
  | Blue -> "blue"

let () =
  print_endline (name Green)

lesson.md: `match` and variants work well together. If you forget a case, the compiler warns you. So when you add a new case to a type, OCaml shows you every `match` that must handle it.

A constructor can carry data. You write the type of the data after `of`. In `Rect of float * float`, the `*` means "and": a `Rect` carries two floats. You create it with a pair in parentheses, `Rect (2.0, 3.0)`, and the pattern `Rect (w, h)` takes the pair apart.

A **record** groups several values, each with a name. These named parts are called **fields**. In the type, each field has a name and a type: `{ name : string; age : int }`. You create a record with `=` for each field, and you read a field with a dot: `p.name`.
A record never changes. `{ p with age = 37 }` creates a copy of `p` in which only `age` is different. The original record stays the same.
Records can also be patterns. `{ x = 0; y = 0 }` fits only that exact point. In `{ x = 0; _ }`, the `_` means that the other fields can have any value.

units.title: Options and more patterns
units.summary: Handle missing values with option, add conditions to patterns with when, and combine lists with List.fold_left.

lesson.md: Sometimes there is no result, for example when you divide by zero. For this, OCaml has the type `option`. An option is either `Some x`, which holds a value `x`, or `None`, which holds nothing. `Some 5` has the type `int option`.
The standard library uses options too. `List.find_opt f list` gives `Some x` with the first element for which `f` gives `true`, or `None` when there is no such element.

lesson.code:
let () =
  let nums = [3; 8; 12; 5] in
  match List.find_opt (fun x -> x > 10) nums with
  | Some x -> Printf.printf "found %d\n" x
  | None -> print_endline "nothing"

lesson.md: An `int option` is not an `int`. `Some 5 + 1` is an error. You must first use `match` to handle both cases. This way, you can never forget the case where the value is missing.
`when` adds a condition to a pattern. The case fits only when the pattern fits and the condition is `true`. In `| x when x < 0`, the name `x` gets the value, and the condition checks it.

lesson.code:
let classify n =
  match n with
  | 0 -> "zero"
  | x when x < 0 -> "negative"
  | x when x mod 2 = 0 -> "even"
  | _ -> "odd"

let () =
  List.iter (fun n -> print_endline (classify n)) [0; -4; 6; 7]

lesson.md: `List.fold_left f start list` combines all elements of a list into one value. The function `f` gets the result so far, called the accumulator, and the next element, and gives the new result. It works like the accumulator from the recursion unit, but you do not write the recursion yourself.

lesson.code:
let () =
  let nums = [1; 2; 3; 4] in
  let total = List.fold_left (fun acc x -> acc + x) 0 nums in
  let biggest = List.fold_left (fun acc x -> if x > acc then x else acc) 0 nums in
  Printf.printf "%d %d\n" total biggest

lesson.md: For `total`, the accumulator starts at `0` and becomes `1`, `3`, `6` and finally `10`. The start value and the result can also be strings or lists.
An operator in parentheses is a function: `( + )` takes two numbers and adds them. So `List.fold_left ( + ) 0 nums` also gives the sum of `nums`.

card: `| x when x > 0 -> ...` adds a condition

exercises.prompt: What does this print?

let () =

  | None -> print_endline "none"
exercises.explain: `9` and `7` are both greater than `5`, but `List.find_opt` gives the first one, `9`.
